A couple of interesting posts in @C_Barraud's packed Thursday Brief indicate that while China’s stock rescue package got a shrug, as I posted on Tuesday, the US midterm results got a rally.

After Beijing rolled out its 2024-style support tools on Monday, the CSI 300 slipped 0.2% Tuesday and the tech-heavy Star 50 fell 3.8%. Then Democrats swept both chambers of Congress, and the CSI 300 jumped 2.3% Wednesday, its best day since July. It added 0.3% Thursday to 4,113, up 2.6% in two sessions.

Hong Kong followed with a bigger move Thursday:
▪️ The Hang Seng rose 3.7%, its best day since February 2025 (+4.0% on February 21, 2025, during the DeepSeek rally). It’s now up about 8% from its October 22 low.
▪️ The Hang Seng Tech rose 5.6%, the most since February 2025, per Bloomberg.
▪️ Alibaba and Tencent each rose more than 7%, and Meituan added 6.8%.

Investors are reading the result as a risk to the US AI hardware trade and rotating into value. China’s internet platforms are about as cheap as large-cap tech gets: Bloomberg notes the Hang Seng Tech traded at 13 times forward earnings last month, the lowest since 2024. Bloomberg Intelligence’s Marvin Chen sees three rotations at once. Money is moving out of Korea and Taiwan into China, into value after China was “stuck at trough valuations” while the rest of the world rallied, and away from “tech hardware and pure AI plays.”

The same rotation shows up in the US. Bespoke says 91.5% of consumer discretionary stocks are above their 50-day averages, the highest in at least a year, compared with 35.5% of tech stocks.

Positioning added fuel. Short selling was 32% of Hong Kong’s turnover on Tuesday, the highest in more than three years, according to Bloomberg. Lotus Asset Management’s Hao Hong calls the move “one of the biggest short squeezes in recent years.” The cost of hedging the Hang Seng Tech fell to its lowest since July, and options volume on the Tracker Fund hit a one-year high as bullish bets dominated.

To be fair to Beijing, Bloomberg also reported stepped-up national-team buying and buybacks Wednesday, so the policy floor is perhaps part of this. 

A caveat: Big up days aren’t reliable bottoms. Since 2000, the Hang Seng has had 53 separate days of 3.5% or more. While a month later it was higher 62% of the time (median +3.0%), three months later it was a coin flip: higher 53% of the time, with a median gain of 1.5%.

That snapped a 46-session streak of more new lows than highs, the longest in at least 17 years of FactSet data, per MarketWatch. 

The Nasdaq improved to -42 from -225, its best since October 6, but it was still its 48th straight negative session, the longest since the 49-day stretch that ended November 14, 2023, according to FactSet.

Citadel's Rubner: The election is over and markets are breathing a sigh of relief... This sets the stage for investors to rebuild equity exposure into year-end.

October brought a significant reset across Technology and the AI complex, but remarkably little broad-based selling… with investors rotating into other parts of the market rather than indiscriminately reducing equity exposure.

The underlying demand picture has also changed. Retail has bought US equities for 22 consecutive sessions (the sixth longest and fifth largest buying streak since 2017 - chart), corporate buyback windows are reopening, and CTA positioning has fallen to -3.3 standard deviations, leaving considerable room for systematic buying as markets recover. 

Meanwhile, earnings continue to beat elevated expectations, while valuations across semiconductors and AI infrastructure have compressed sharply.

We believe the combination of light positioning, returning corporate demand, persistent retail buying, and historically favorable post-midterm seasonality creates a compelling setup for US equities into year-end. With the election behind us and volatility potentially normalizing, there is considerable capacity for investors to rebuild risk.

Inflation has more than wiped out all US consumer wage gains since the 2020 Pandemic:

US consumer prices have risen +31.3% since April 2020, to an all-time high in September.

Over the same period, average hourly earnings have increased just +25.9%.

This comes as CPI inflation has now been above the Fed’s 2% target for 67 consecutive months, the 3rd-longest streak over the last 100 years.

The only 2 longer streaks lasted 242 months, ending in 1986, and 128 months, ending in 1997.

Inflation continues to erode the spending power of Americans.

I can only reply to a minority of comments, and it’s usually luck-of-the-draw what I see when I’m online. And Twitter isn’t really the best place for long-form debates.

“Why do you think the legal system couldn’t prevent the Biden Admin from allowing millions of unknown foreign men to illegally enter the country?”

-Surely you’re aware of the asymmetry that courts are more able to block specific illegal actions than force officials to take positive actions that require funding. In other words, with a stroke of a pen a court can say,“no, those tariffs are illegal actually, you can’t use emergency powers for indefinite and broad new taxes” but it’s much harder to say, “you have to allocate more resources to the border.” To fix the latter you generally need an executive and legislative branch with the will to do it, which is partially what the 2024 election was a mandate on.

“Why can’t the legal system prevent criminals who’ve been arrested 37 times from being let back into society?”

-Places where people are arrested 37 times tend to be cities where the politicians and courts are in agreement. That’s the set of policies they have on the books and how the rules are being interpreted. If people get fed up with it they can elect people that will write and interpret stricter laws and sentences about repeated crime.

“Why couldn’t the legal system prevent billions of dollars of egregious welfare fraud?”

-Tons of cases are prosecuted each year. Even so, outright fraud is a small share of the spending. The bigger issue is healthcare bloat and demographics.

“Why can’t the legal system enact voter ID which is the most obvious and basic tenet of election security?”

-It’s not the role of the legal system to enact voter ID or other details around voting. That’s primarily within the legislative branch (unless the legislative branch does something that violates the Constitution).

“If you are so willing to label Trump a "fascist", perhaps you could assign a label to the people who fail to deliver the most basic functions of government? What label should they be given?”

-By definition, that description would be closer to anarchist.

tweets.text:
Huge relief for $MARA.

FERC approved $MARA’s Long Ridge acquisition today (EC26-92). Good to see the IMM’s spurious BlackRock/Vanguard challenge get the Heisman. FERC also turned down the request to condition approval on keeping the plant’s output in PJM. Solid.

The deal: $1.512B enterprise value for ~0.5 GW of gas generation (485 MW authorized, 505 MW nameplate) and ~$144M of annualized adj. EBITDA, about 10.5x. Recent PJM gas plant deals went at about 7x (Talen 6.7x, Vistra 7x, NRG 7.5x), which would put the plant alone at ~$1.0B. MARA is paying ~$0.5B more for the land, gas wells, rail and expansion option. MARA keeps ~$900M of Long Ridge debt in place and needs ~$610M of cash, which the $600M of BTC-backed loans it drew in August are meant to cover. I’d expect it to close by the Nov 30 outside date.

Debt math: ~$1.9B of MARA’s $2.3B convert stack is zero coupon, so total post-close cash interest is roughly $140M: ~$58M on the Coinbase and Two Prime loans, ~$76M on Long Ridge’s own debt (the 8.75% notes alone are $52.5M) and ~$7M on the converts. Judging the deal on its own: the debt that finances it (Long Ridge’s ~$76M plus ~$46M on the new BTC loans) costs ~$123M a year against $144M of EBITDA, about 1.2x. The upside is expansion.

MARA talks about 600 gross MW of AI load at the site. That appears to include the existing 200 MW of grid load (on top of the 505 MW plant that sells into PJM). AEP’s 2025 filing proposed reconductoring the feeder serving a customer at the Hannibal station to go from 100 to 200 MW, for about $0.5M, targeting about nine months from PJM first seeing the need to in-service. The station ties into four 138 kV lines and once fed a 540 MW smelter, which is encouraging, but nothing is signed. To get from 200 to 600 MW, AEP would likely need to add a second feed or upgrade lines, or MARA would build on-site generation, which raises turbine availability questions. I can’t find a public study of how much more the grid connection can carry. AEP Ohio’s data center tariff also requires large customers to pay for at least 85% of contracted capacity for up to 12 years, if it applies here. Still, an energized site with fuel, land and a 138 kV hub may beat waiting in ERCOT’s queue.

It’s unclear whether the Hannibal buildout goes through the Starwood JV, where MARA would keep up to 50%. That will decide how much of the 600 MW upside MARA owns. Each 100MW developed at a 7% cap rate and $2M/MW rent could be $1.5B+ of value creation, so it's a big variable and explains why they paid ~$500M above the 7x multiple for the extra capacity.

Next catalyst, possibly at closing or just after: a signed lease.

tweets.text:
High-income workers are fleeing Europe. 

Economic theory tells us that the more
mobile a factor of production becomes,
the lower its optimal tax rate. This is why taxes on capital, which is relatively mobile, tend to be lower than taxes on labor, which historically has been less mobile.

However, as the chart below shows, as elite human capital has become more footloose, high taxes have become increasingly counterproductive.

This is a huge existential problem for European welfare states, which have traditionally relied on heavily taxing their most productive workers.

tweets.text: If the increase in money supply was matched by an increase in productive capacity, real incomes would be higher, and there wouldn't be a cost-of-living crisis. An increase in money supply for unproductive uses, namely financing a massive property bubble, plus deficit spending by governments- the one entity you do not want to give free rein to- results in terminal decline, removal of rights, a march towards authoritarianism, and economic collapse.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
In 1995, Australia’s M3 money supply was approximately $309 billion. By September 2026, it has reached almost $3.5 trillion.

That’s an increase of more than 1,000%. When money and credit expand faster than our ability to produce goods, build houses and deliver services, https://t.co/CR98VqrzZy
